title.rendered: Healthy Travel Snacks for Flights and Train Journeys: What to Pack and What to Skip

content.rendered:
Anyone who has paid ₹250 for a limp sandwich at the boarding gate knows the feeling. You're hungry, the options are limited, and whatever is in front of you is expensive, oily, or both. Trains are no kinder. A pantry car samosa at hour nine of a long journey is rarely a happy memory.

Packing your own healthy travel snacks fixes this, but only if you pick the right ones. Plenty of foods that sound sensible at home turn into a mess, a smell or a soggy lump by the time you reach your seat. This guide covers what works on flights and trains, what doesn't, and how to pack so you arrive feeling fine.

What Makes Healthy Travel Snacks Work?

Snacking at home and snacking on the move are different problems. At home you have a plate, a sink and a fridge. In seat 14C you have none of those. So the best healthy travel snacks share a few traits.

  • Dry and mess-free. You should be able to eat them one-handed without needing a napkin.
  • No refrigeration. Anything that needs to stay cold is a gamble after a couple of hours.
  • A mild smell. Your seatmate shares your air, and strong smells get noticed fast in a closed space.
  • Light and compact. Weight adds up when you're also carrying a laptop bag and a water bottle.
  • Some fibre or protein. Pure sugar gives you a quick lift and leaves you hungry again an hour later.

None of this is complicated, yet most packed snacks fail at least two of these tests.

Flights and Trains Need Different Snacks

Journey length changes what you should carry, so it helps to plan for each separately.

On a flight

A Kolkata to Delhi flight takes about two and a quarter hours. That's short enough that you mostly need something to stop you buying overpriced airport food, and to cover delays. Solid, dry snacks generally pass through security without trouble, but rules vary by airline and airport, so check yours before you leave. Liquids and gels fall under the usual cabin limits, which rules out dips and spreads.

Smell matters most here. A full cabin has no windows to open, so mild flavours are the polite choice. Cabin air is also dry, which leaves you thirstier than usual, and heavily salted snacks can make that worse. Carry water either way.

On a train

The train is the opposite problem. Journeys of twelve hours or more are normal, and some take most of a day. You'll eat several times, you'll get bored, and you'll want variety. This is where a mix of flavours earns its place.

You also have more room to breathe, so a stronger flavour is easier to get away with. Your compartment might disagree if it's garlic at 6 a.m. Station food is a lottery, sometimes excellent and sometimes not, and a backup in your bag means you can skip the bad days.

Foods That Look Healthy but Travel Badly

Some popular choices cause more trouble than they're worth.

  • Cut fruit. It browns, leaks and attracts attention. Whole apples travel fine. Bananas bruise in a crowded bag.
  • Anything with curd. Chaas, raita and curd sandwiches turn risky after a few hours in a warm bag.
  • Fried snacks in healthy packaging. "Multigrain" does not mean "not fried", so read the label.
  • Protein bars heavy on syrup. Some contain as much sugar as a chocolate bar.
  • Boiled eggs. Good nutrition, brutal on a shared journey. I'd leave them at home.

Where Makhana Fits In

Makhana, also called fox nuts, ticks most of the boxes above. It's dry, airy and weighs almost nothing. Korigo roasts its flavoured makhana slowly over a low flame instead of frying it, uses no palm oil, and lists about 380 kcal and 9.7g of plant protein per 100g. The brand's own comparison puts fried chips at 560 kcal or more. It is also vegetarian and gluten free, which keeps things simple if you're travelling with a group.

Keep expectations realistic, though. Going by those per-100g figures, a 35g pack works out to roughly 130 kcal and about 3g of protein. That's a light snack, not a meal. For a long journey, pair it with something more filling, like a sandwich or a handful of plain nuts.

One practical point: makhana is crunchy because it's full of air, so it can crush if a heavy bag sits on it. Keep your packs in a front pocket, not under the laptop.

A Flavour Guide for Travel

Korigo has six flavours. Here's how they match up to a trip. This is judgement, not science, so adjust it to your own taste.

Flavour Taste Best for Note

Cinnamon Drip Sweet roasted Flights Mild, and it handles a sweet craving
Sour Crème d' Onion Creamy herbs Trains Gentle on heat, but you'll smell the onion
Garlicked Cheese Savoury crunch Trains Garlic carries, so skip it in a tight cabin
Sassy Sriracha Spicy heat Trains Keep water handy
Coco Island Chocolate glaze Either Keep it out of direct sun and heat

For long trips, the are the sensible buy. Each duo costs ₹158 against ₹198 for two single packs, and you get two flavours to rotate through. If you plan to before a trip, order a few days ahead. Korigo dispatches same day for orders placed before 2 PM, but courier times vary by city.

How Much Should You Pack?

A rough rule is one 35g pack for every two to three hours of travel, plus one spare. For a two-hour flight, that's one pack and a backup in case of delay. For an overnight train, plan on six or more and mix the flavours so you don't tire of one. Delays are common on both, and an extra pack costs very little.

Packing Tips That Help

  • Keep snacks in your personal bag, not in checked luggage, so they're in reach when you're hungry.
  • Use a small zip pouch to contain crumbs and stop packs migrating to the bottom of the bag.
  • Carry water, especially on flights.
  • Eat on a schedule. Planned snacking beats panic buying at the platform.
  • Carry one mild flavour and one bold flavour so you can choose by mood and by who's sitting next to you.

FAQs

What are the best healthy travel snacks for a flight?

Dry, low-smell foods that need no refrigeration. Roasted makhana in mild flavours, whole fruit and plain nuts all work. Avoid liquids and anything with a strong smell.

Can I carry flavoured makhana on a train or flight?

It's a sealed, dry, solid snack, so trains are rarely a problem. On flights, packaged solid snacks are normally fine in cabin bags, but check your airline and airport rules before you travel.

Is makhana filling enough for a long journey?

On its own, it's a light snack. For a long trip, pair it with something more substantial and keep the makhana for between meals.

Pack Smarter, Eat Better on the Road

Good healthy travel snacks are boring in the best way: dry, mild, light and easy to eat without thinking. Work out your quantities, mix your flavours, keep water nearby, and you can skip the gate-side sandwich. Browse, pick a couple that suit your journey, and put them in the front pocket.

title.rendered: Is Makhana Safe During Pregnancy? Benefits & Side Effects

content.rendered:
Makhana in pregnancy is a very useful snack when taken in moderation and in its roasted form. Makhana taken in its roasted form without any flavouring is usually seen as a food item that can be consumed in the diet of pregnant women, although individual requirements may vary. This guide gives all details about the quantity to take, its nutritional value, advantages and disadvantages, and more.

Korigo Snacks advocates that good snacks should be about tasteful decisions. The roasted makhana we produce is suitable as a snack food, but pregnant women need to look at the nutrition facts of any before including it in their daily diet.

Is Makhana Safe in Pregnancy?

Makhana, or fox nuts/gorgon nuts, are popped seeds or kernels of an aquatic plant, Euryale ferox. The nuts contain carbohydrates, along with proteins, fibre, and minerals in small quantities:

There is no specific FSSAI or ICMR guideline that individually mentions makhana as either safe or unsafe during pregnancy.

The general advice provided by FSSAI about pregnancy nutrition suggests a balanced and healthy diet, and no food must be prohibited during pregnancy.

The ICMR provides information on food composition but not specifically about pregnancy nutrition safety.

There is a lack of pregnancy-specific studies on the use of normal food amounts of makhana. Thus, it is more appropriate to define it as a food product that may be incorporated into a healthy diet.

Can Makhana Cause Miscarriage?

No credible scientific evidence has been found showing that consumption of normal amounts of simple roasted makhana results in miscarriage.

Nutrition in Makhana (Per 30 g)

have been identified from its supply of carbohydrates, fibre, and lesser amounts of protein and minerals. But such benefits must be seen as dietary support during pregnancy and not as any form of medication.

These figures represent an approximation for 30 g based on the typical food composition of plain makhana from India. The nutritional value may differ depending on the variety of makhana.

Nutrient Approx. per 30 g Why it matters in pregnancy
Calories ~104 kcal Source of energy as part of a balanced snack
Protein ~2.9 g Contributes to higher protein requirements
Carbohydrates ~23.1 g Contributes to energy provision but must be considered in terms of a carbohydrate-restricted diet
Fibre ~4.4 g Assists in proper bowel movement
Calcium ~18 mg Contributes to bone and tooth formation requirements
Magnesium ~20 mg Contributes to appropriate muscle and nerve function
Potassium ~150 mg Helps proper fluid balance and muscle function
Iron ~0.4 mg Offers an insignificant amount to the iron content.

Benefits of Makhana in Pregnancy

The consumption of makhana may be considered as a good substitute for some other fried and heavily processed foods if it is dry-roasted or lightly cooked. The nutritive value of makhana lies primarily in the carbohydrates that it contains, along with a lesser amount of protein, fibre and minerals. But these advantages need to be taken in the context of a balanced diet during pregnancy.

Plant Protein and Calcium for Bone Health

Makhana offers a little bit of protein and calcium. This contributes to the total intake requirement for the general well-being of pregnant women and proper bone and tissue development; however, makhana on its own does not satisfy the need for protein and calcium during pregnancy.

Magnesium and Potassium for Proper Functioning of Muscles and Blood Pressure Regulation

The magnesium and potassium found in makhana contribute to the normal functioning of muscles, nerves, and fluids. A balanced diet that includes potassium-rich foods is good for heart health, but makhana cannot be used to treat hypertension or pregnancy-related cramps.

Fibre for Constipation

Makhana offers some fibre, which promotes digestion. During pregnancy, when constipation becomes a problem, fibre-filled snacks like makhana are helpful in addition to drinking lots of water and a balanced diet of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and pulses.

A Convenient Snack for Cravings and Blood Sugar Control

Plain roasted makhana can be a good choice as an alternative to sweet or deep-fried snacks. But keep in mind that it still has considerable carbohydrates, which means that people with gestational diabetes should account for it in their daily carb intake.

Lower-Fat and Lower-Calorie Versus Fried Snacks

Plain makhana is naturally very low in fat compared to many fried snacks. So, when you choose dry-roasted makhana instead of oil-coated variants, you can get a healthier snack.

A Small Contribution of Iron

Makhana has some iron, but the quantity in a standard serving is not too impressive. Thus, it can be considered only as a small source of iron in the diet, not as a substitute for prescribed iron supplements and foods rich in iron.

What Makhana Does Not Do

Makhana does not treat anaemia, constipation, gestational diabetes, high blood pressure or any other pregnancy-related conditions. Instead, it can be used as one element of a diverse diet, and the medical issues need to be addressed based on the advice of a doctor.

Simple include roasted makhana with a sprinkle of rock salt, makhana and yoghurt, a homemade trail mix or sweetened makhana kheer.

Side Effects and Risks of Makhana in Pregnancy

Makhana is usually a basic food product, but consuming it in excessive amounts or opting for highly seasoned varieties can lead to avoidable issues. Most worries pertain to the quantity of the consumption.

Bloatedness and Bloating

Consuming a large volume of food in one go could result in bloating or gas formation, especially if there are difficulties with digestion owing to pregnancy. Take a smaller volume if it does not come easy to you.

Constipation

Consuming a lot of fibre but little water might lead to constipation. Ensure that you drink enough water and consume other foods rich in fibre apart from consuming just makhana.

Salt and Oil Content in Packaged Products

Fried makhana might consist of high levels of salt, oil, sugar, dairy products, and other components used for taste-making. Those who have been advised to limit their intake of salt might find such products unsuitable.

Allergy

While makhana is not a nut, just a seed, allergic reactions may occur in some people. In case you have never tasted makhana, try to eat small quantities and do not continue consuming it if any allergic reaction signs appear.

Gestational Diabetes

It is necessary to understand that makhana is not free from carbohydrates. If you have gestational diabetes, you should count it as a carbohydrate product and follow the diet recommended by your doctor.

How Much Makhana Can You Eat in Pregnancy?

No established dose has been found specifically for makhana in pregnancy. The following values are general portion recommendations, not official medical dosages.

Portion Practical Use
15-20 g Lower quantity if you suffer from nausea or lack of appetite or are trying makhana for the first time
30-40 g Reasonable standard range of the snack quantity for most people
50-70 g Larger quantity; beware of bloating, stomach upset, and total carbohydrate consumption
80 g or more Should be avoided as standard quantity for one-time snack consumption

Drink a lot of water throughout the day, especially if you are increasing your intake of fibre.

Makhana in Trimesters

First Trimester

Small quantities will be easier on the stomach if there is poor appetite and/or morning sickness. Stick to unsalted, lightly roasted makhana, and consume only if the taste and aroma do not pose a problem for you.

Second Trimester

With increasing nutrient needs, makhana can provide small quantities of calcium, magnesium and protein. The snack should not substitute healthier meals but act as an addition to a healthy and varied diet.

Third Trimester

Make sure to monitor portions, hydration, digestive issues and sodium in packaged versions.

Who Should Be Careful or Check With Their Doctor

Discuss with your doctor or a certified dietitian the inclusion of makhana as a regular snack if you suffer from gestational diabetes, hypertension, oedema, chronic constipation, IBS, or an allergy to seeds and nuts.

Best Ways to Eat Makhana During Pregnancy

One method would be eating dry-roasted makhana with a dash of rock salt or any other mild seasoning. Another one involves mixing roasted makhana into yoghurt or creating a homemade trail mix. Makhana kheer that uses milk and reduced amounts of sugar would be another choice.

Improved Preparation Methods

  • Dry or slightly roasted instead of deep-fried
  • Unsalted or slightly salted instead of highly salted
  • Flavoured makhana, with care about salt content and other additives
  • Makhana kheer prepared with milk and some amount of sugar
  • Alongside yoghurt or part of a home-prepared trail mix

It is recommended that you buy fresh and clean makhana from a reputable source and store it in an airtight box in a cool and dry place.

Makhana During Pregnancy: A Healthy Choice in Moderation

Roasted makhana without any added ingredients can be considered a good makhana in pregnancy. Nevertheless, it is advised to take it in moderation along with a well-balanced diet.

As far as Korigo Snacks is concerned, our products emphasise the use of , which is both tasty and healthy. For pregnant women, one may consider makhana for regular consumption, making sure of the individual ingredients used in flavours and amounts.

For gestational diabetes, swelling, high blood pressure, digestion issues or an allergy to makhana, you need to consult your gynaecologist or nutritionist.

FAQs

Can I eat makhana every day in pregnancy?

Yes. Regular consumption of plain roasted makhana is fine in moderation if it fits your diet and your doctor has not restricted you from consuming it. A reasonable amount is about 30 g.

Is makhana safe in the first trimester?

Simple roasted makhana may be safely taken during the first trimester in moderation, provided one is not nauseous or repulsive to the taste.

Can makhana cause miscarriage?

There is no scientific evidence available about the normal quantity of plain roasted makhana resulting in miscarriage. However, there is not much scientific research about the use of makhana in pregnant women; therefore, it should be taken as a food and not a medicine.

Is makhana good for gestational diabetes?

Makhana can form part of some dietary plans for gestational diabetes patients, but it does contain carbohydrates. The serving amount and the rest of the meal count, so you should observe the amounts of carbs recommended by your doctor or dietitian.

Can I eat roasted or flavoured makhana?

Plain makhana is always the better option. Flavoured makhana might include additional ingredients such as salt, sugar, oil, milk, soy, nuts, or any other ingredients that might trigger allergies, so take care to read the label.

Makhana nutritional value per 100g will be determined based on how the seeds are taken. The nutritional content per 100g of makhana is likely to include 347-360 kcal and 9.7-10.5g of protein. How Many Calories Are in Makhana?

Makhana has an appreciable amount of calories per 100g, but the serving size of makhana eaten by an individual is usually lower than that. Roasted dry makhana gives around 360 kcal per 100g, and the calories in 30g of it will be about 108. Thus, eating a handful of makhana could give approximately 90-110 kcal.

The processing method makes a lot of difference. For instance, the ghee-roasted version can have around 420 kcal per 100g, while oil-roasted or highly flavoured ones could have up to 450-480 kcal.

Makhana Protein Value: Is It Enough?

Makhana contains about 9.7 to 10.5g of protein per 100g; that means 3.2g in 30g of makhana. Makhana can be a good source of protein but not a high-protein food. In fact, roasted chana, peanuts, and almonds contain more protein per 100g.

Makhana protein cannot be regarded as a complete source of protein. To have a more varied spectrum of amino acids, one should combine makhana with foods like milk, curd, nuts, seeds, or sprouts.

Carbs, Fibre and Glycaemic Index

Makhana is mainly composed of carbohydrates, with 77g per 100g in Indian food composition databases. Makhana also consists of fibre; nevertheless, there are varying levels of the amount of fibre, depending on different food composition databases. The glycaemic index of makhana is estimated to be between 55 and 65. Makhana is gluten-free.

Vitamins and Minerals in Makhana

Makhana is an excellent source of various minerals like calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, potassium, and iron. One 32g portion of dried lotus seeds contains 52mg of calcium, 67mg of magnesium, 200mg of phosphorus, 438mg of potassium, and 1.13mg of iron. Additionally, makhana is a good source of antioxidants that include flavonoids and phenolics, like gallic acid.

Health Benefits of Makhana (What the Evidence Shows)

Makhana is an edible item packed with nutrients such as protein, fibre, and antioxidants, among others. can be beneficial for satiety and nutrition, provided that they are taken in the right amounts:

Weight Management

Since makhana contains fibre, some amount of protein and not a high amount of fat, it can be a healthy snack. But its portion size must be controlled because calories will increase significantly when ghee, oil, sugar or other coatings are used in it.

Blood Sugar

Though the GI value of makhana is rather moderate, and it contains some fiber, we need to treat claims about the ability of makhana to help in lowering blood sugar with some reservation, since a lot of studies supporting its therapeutic properties were conducted in laboratories or on animals.

Heart Health

Potassium and magnesium contained in makhana, as well as its low-fat nature, can make it a healthy food. But there is no evidence of any effect of makhana on prevention of cardiovascular diseases in humans.

Bones and Skin

Calcium, magnesium and phosphorus help in bone development. There are also antioxidants, which can prevent cells from oxidation, but it is still unclear whether they can be used for treating diseases.

How Much Makhana Should You Eat Daily?

An appropriate serving size is about 30-50g per day. Individuals seeking should keep their portions small and opt for plain or mildly roasted varieties. However, caloric consumption will remain significant in managing weight.

Side Effects and Who Should Be Careful

Consumption of excessive amounts of makhana may result in bloating or indigestion. Individuals suffering from kidney stone problems must consult a healthcare provider about regular intake due to oxalate content in makhana. Individuals suffering from chronic kidney disease must be cautious of their phosphorus and potassium intake as well. Salted and flavoured variants of makhana have high salt, fat, and oil content.

Makhana Nutritional Value Per 100g: What Should You Take Care Of?

At Korigo Snacks, our speciality is roasted makhana, a delicious snack with a delightful combination of texture, taste and convenience. Our nutritional facts reveal that makhana has around 8% to 10% protein and 5% to 8% fibre content, with variations in nutritional facts according to flavours. If convenience is what you desire, then and compare their nutritional values.

Knowledge of makhana nutritional value per 100g will assist you to make better choices on how much and how you prepare the food. Roasted makhana is an ideal snack, but flavoured makhana may require checking additional content such as oil and salt.

FAQs

Is makhana good for weight loss?

It can work well within a controlled-calorie diet provided that it is consumed in reasonable portions. One could use makhana for losing weight as a substitute for fried snacks although calorie consumption is still vital in general.

Is makhana good for diabetics?

Roasted makhana without any additions can be part of a diabetic diet, but it depends on how much of it you consume.

Is makhana a complete protein?

No. It is a source of protein, but it needs to be supplemented with additional protein-containing foods.

Raw or roasted—which is healthier?

Dry-roasted makhana with moderate amounts of oil is usually a reasonable choice as a snack. Any added ghee, sugar, oil or salt alters its nutritional value.

Does makhana increase uric acid?

There is no reliable information regarding raising uric acid levels due to ordinary portions of makhana. Medical recommendations depend on specific health problems.

Is makhana gluten-free?

Yes. Makhana is a gluten-free product by nature and can therefore be used by people with gluten intolerance.

title.rendered: Late Night Healthy Snacks That Won’t Make You Feel Guilty

content.rendered:
Late-night hunger does not necessarily mean that you are messing up with your diet plan. title.rendered: Healthy Makhana Recipes You Can Make at Home

content.rendered:
If you've been staring at a bag of fox nuts wondering what to actually do with them beyond roasting and salting, you're not alone. Makhana has quietly become one of those snacks everyone knows is "good for you" but nobody quite knows how to cook. It shows up in Ayurvedic texts, in postpartum diets across North India, and now in every fitness influencer's pantry – yet most people's makhana repertoire begins and ends with a basic roast.

That's a shame, because makhana recipes are genuinely versatile. The seed itself (technically the popped seed of the Euryale ferox plant, also called fox nut or lotus seed) has a mild, almost neutral flavour and a light, crunchy texture that takes on whatever you pair it with. It's low in fat, naturally gluten-free, and carries a decent dose of protein and magnesium per serving – which is part of why it's turned up in weight-management diets and diabetic-friendly meal plans over the last few years.

This guide walks through practical, kitchen-tested ways to cook makhana at home, why it deserves a permanent spot in your snack rotation, and a few flavour directions if you'd rather skip the cooking altogether.

What Makes Makhana Worth Cooking With

Before getting into recipes, it helps to understand why makhana keeps showing up in nutrition conversations. A 100-gram serving of roasted makhana has roughly 350 calories, close to 9-10 grams of protein, and very little fat compared to most fried snacks. It's also a reasonable source of calcium and magnesium, two minerals that don't always get enough attention in typical Indian diets.

None of this makes makhana a miracle food – no single ingredient is. But swapped in for chips, namkeen, or fried mixture, it's a straightforward way to cut down on oil and refined carbs without giving up the satisfaction of a crunchy snack. Dietitians often recommend it for evening hunger pangs specifically because the fibre content helps keep you full longer than most packaged alternatives.

Basic Roasted Makhana (The Foundation Recipe)

Every other makhana recipe builds on this one, so it's worth getting right.

What you need: 2 cups of makhana, 1 tablespoon ghee or oil, salt to taste, a pinch of turmeric (optional, for colour).

Method: Heat the ghee in a heavy-bottomed pan on low flame. Add the makhana and stir constantly – this part matters, because unroasted makhana still has a soft, slightly rubbery centre, and uneven heat leaves you with some pieces crunchy and others chewy. Roast for 8-10 minutes until they turn a light golden colour and sound hollow when tapped with a spoon. Sprinkle salt and turmeric, toss well, and let them cool completely before storing. They'll turn soggy if sealed while still warm.

This base roast is where most home cooks stop. But once you've got the technique down, it's easy to branch out.

Five Ways to Flavour Your Makhana

Once the base roast is sorted, flavouring is really just a matter of what spice mix you toss it in while it's still hot from the pan – that's when the seasoning sticks best.

Sweet and warm: A dusting of powdered jaggery, a little ghee, and cinnamon turns roasted makhana into something closer to a dessert than a snack. If you'd rather not measure and mix at home, our cinnamon flavoured makhana does this exact combination, minus the guesswork.

Bright and tangy: Lemon zest, chaat masala, and a touch of black salt give makhana a sharp, palate-cleansing edge – good for humid afternoons when a heavy snack feels like too much. This is the flavour profile behind our citrus flavoured makhana.

Rich and indulgent: Cocoa powder, a little jaggery syrup, and a pinch of sea salt make a surprisingly convincing chocolate-coated makhana, best eaten within a day or two before the coating softens. We sell a version of this too – the chocolate flavoured makhana – for the days you don't feel like tempering cocoa yourself.

Savoury and sharp: Garlic powder, dried herbs, and grated cheese (or nutritional yeast, for a vegan version) baked onto the makhana for a few extra minutes gives you something close to a healthier nacho substitute. If that sounds appealing but sounds like a lot of steps, the garlic cheese makhana skips straight to the eating part.

Fiery and bold: For people who want heat, a sriracha-based glaze brushed on toward the end of roasting (add it too early and it burns) gives makhana a genuinely spicy kick without deep-frying anything. Our spicy sriracha flavoured makhana is built around this exact idea.

Classic and comforting: If none of the above appeal and you just want something reminiscent of sour cream and onion chips, a mix of onion powder, a little citric acid, and dried chives gets close. We make a packaged version of this too, in our cream and onion makhana range.

Makhana Kheer (For When You Want Something Warm)

This is the recipe most Bengali and North Indian households already know, usually made for festivals or given to new mothers.

What you need: 1 cup makhana, 1 litre full-fat milk, 3-4 tablespoons sugar or jaggery, a handful of chopped almonds and cashews, a few strands of saffron, and a pinch of cardamom powder.

Method: Dry-roast the makhana in a pan until crisp, then set aside a handful for garnish and roughly crush the rest. Bring the milk to a boil, lower the heat, and let it simmer for 15-20 minutes until it reduces slightly and thickens. Add the crushed makhana and cook for another 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally so it doesn't stick to the bottom. Stir in sugar, saffron, and cardamom, and simmer for a final 5 minutes. Top with the reserved whole makhana and chopped nuts before serving, warm or chilled.

This one's less of a snack and more of a dessert, but it's a good reminder that makhana isn't only for the evening-tea crowd.

Makhana Curry (A North Indian Sabzi)

Less common outside Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, but worth trying if you want makhana as part of an actual meal rather than a snack.

What you need: 1.5 cups makhana, 1 tablespoon ghee, 1 chopped onion, 1 tomato pureed, 1 teaspoon ginger-garlic paste, ½ cup cashew paste (for creaminess), turmeric, red chilli powder, garam masala, and salt.

Method: Lightly roast the makhana in ghee and set aside – this keeps them from turning mushy in the gravy. In the same pan, sauté the onion until golden, add ginger-garlic paste, then the tomato puree and spices, cooking until the oil separates from the masala. Stir in the cashew paste for the body, add a cup of water, and simmer for 5 minutes. Add the roasted makhana back in, mix gently, and cook for another 3-4 minutes so they soak up some of the gravy without going soft all the way through. Serve with roti or steamed rice.

Storage Tips That Actually Matter

Makhana absorbs moisture fast, which is the main reason home-roasted batches go stale within a week while packaged versions last months. A few things help: always cool the roasted makhana fully before sealing it, store it in an airtight glass or steel container rather than plastic bags, and keep it away from direct sunlight or stove heat. If you live somewhere humid – coastal cities especially – adding a small silica packet or a spoon of dry rice to the container can buy you a few extra days of crunch.

When You'd Rather Skip the Cooking

Not every evening allows for roasting spices and babysitting a pan. That’s a fair trade-off ,and honestly it’s kind of the whole reason why flavoured ready to eat makhana even exists as a category in the first place, you know. Whether you're after something sweet like the cinnamon version, something with real heat like the sriracha one, or a savoury option like garlic cheese, having a few packs on hand covers the days when cooking from scratch just isn't happening.

Makhana isn't going to replace every snack in your kitchen, and it shouldn't have to. But between the roasted basics, the kheer, the curry, and the flavoured options for lazier days, there's enough range here that it doesn't have to be boring either.

Frequently Asked Questions:

Is makhana good for weight loss? 

It can help, mainly because it's low in fat and high in fibre compared to fried snacks, so it tends to keep you full on fewer calories. It's not a fat-burning food on its own – portion size still matters, especially with the ghee-roasted versions.

Can diabetics eat makhana? 

Plain roasted makhana has a relatively low glycemic index and is often recommended in moderation as a snack alternative for people managing blood sugar. Sweetened versions, like jaggery or chocolate-coated makhana, should be eaten more carefully and in smaller portions.

How much makhana should I eat in a day? 

A handful, roughly 30-40 grams, is a reasonable daily serving for most adults. Eating significantly more than that regularly can add up in calories, especially if it's roasted in a generous amount of ghee.

Why does my home-roasted makhana go soft quickly? 

Usually it's one of two things: the makhana wasn't roasted long enough to crisp all the way through, or it was sealed in a container before fully cooling. Both trap moisture, which softens the texture within a day or two.

Is makhana the same as popcorn? 

No, despite similar snacking use. Makhana comes from the seed of the prickly water lily plant and is roasted, not popped from kernels like popcorn. The nutritional profile is different too – makhana generally has more protein and less starch per serving.
